claim: RCK domains regulate the activity of K+ channels and transporters in eukaryotic and prokaryotic organisms by responding to ions or nucleotides.
source: RCK domains regulate the activity of K+ channels and transporters in eukaryotic and prokaryotic organisms by responding to ions or nucleotides.
evidence: This is a general statement about RCK domain function supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The mechanisms of RCK activation by Ca2+ in the eukaryotic BK and bacterial MthK K+ channels are well understood.
source: The mechanisms of RCK activation by Ca2+ in the eukaryotic BK and bacterial MthK K+ channels are well understood.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research throughout the manuscript.

claim: The molecular details of activation in nucleotide-dependent RCK domains are not clear.
source: However, the molecular details of activation in nucleotide-dependent RCK domains are not clear.
evidence: This represents a knowledge gap that the study aims to address.

claim: Activation of KtrA by nucleotide requires binding of cations to an intra-dimer interface site in the RCK dimer.
source: Through a functional and structural analysis of the mechanism of ATP activation in KtrA, a RCK domain from the B. subtilis KtrAB cation channel, we have found that activation by nucleotide requires binding of cations to an intra-dimer interface site in the RCK dimer.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by structural and functional data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Divalent cations are coordinated by the γ-phosphates of bound-ATP, tethering the two subunits and stabilizing the active state conformation.
source: In particular, divalent cations are coordinated by the γ-phosphates of bound-ATP, tethering the two subunits and stabilizing the active state conformation.
evidence: This is supported by structural data showing magnesium and calcium coordination at the intra-dimer interface.

claim: The binding site residues are highly conserved in many different nucleotide-dependent RCK domains.
source: Strikingly, the binding site residues are highly conserved in many different nucleotide-dependent RCK domains, indicating that divalent cations are a general cofactor in the regulatory mechanism of many nucleotide-dependent RCK domains.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment analysis presented in Figure 11 and supplementary figures.

claim: Divalent cations are a general cofactor in the regulatory mechanism of many nucleotide-dependent RCK domains.
source: Strikingly, the binding site residues are highly conserved in many different nucleotide-dependent RCK domains, indicating that divalent cations are a general cofactor in the regulatory mechanism of many nucleotide-dependent RCK domains.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the conservation analysis and structural data.

claim: RCK domains regulate the function of the eukaryotic Slo K+ channels.
source: These domains regulate the function of the eukaryotic Slo K+ channels (Jiang et al., 2001), with roles in neuronal excitability, smooth muscle contractility, hormone secretion, nociception and fertility (Barrett et al., 1982; Lu et al., 2015; Raffaelli et al., 2004; Santi et al., 2010; Tabak et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Slo K+ channels have roles in neuronal excitability, smooth muscle contractility, hormone secretion, nociception and fertility.
source: These domains regulate the function of the eukaryotic Slo K+ channels (Jiang et al., 2001), with roles in neuronal excitability, smooth muscle contractility, hormone secretion, nociception and fertility (Barrett et al., 1982; Lu et al., 2015; Raffaelli et al., 2004; Santi et al., 2010; Tabak et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: RCK domains are commonly found as regulatory domains of prokaryotic K+ channels and transporters.
source: RCK domains are also commonly found as regulatory domains of prokaryotic K+ channels and transporters, with key roles in osmoregulation, pH homeostasis, regulation of turgor pressure and membrane potential (Bakker and Mangerich, 1981; Epstein and Schultz, 1965; Kroll and Booth, 1981; Meury et al., 1985; Whatmore and Reed, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: More than half of the identified prokaryotic K+ channels contain RCK domains.
source: Attesting to the importance of these domains for K+ homeostasis in prokaryotes, more than half of the identified prokaryotic K+ channels contain RCK domains (Kuo et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: RCK domains form dimeric or pseudo-dimeric units.
source: RCK domains form dimeric or pseudo-dimeric units (Jiang et al., 2001; Wu et al., 2010; Yuan et al., 2010), which assemble as functional octameric rings (Albright et al., 2006; Jiang et al., 2002; Wu et al., 2010; Yuan et al., 2010); the KefC K+ transporter is an exception, with a RCK domain dimer as the functional unit (Roosild et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior structural studies.

claim: RCK dimeric units assemble as functional octameric rings.
source: RCK domains form dimeric or pseudo-dimeric units (Jiang et al., 2001; Wu et al., 2010; Yuan et al., 2010), which assemble as functional octameric rings (Albright et al., 2006; Jiang et al., 2002; Wu et al., 2010; Yuan et al., 2010); the KefC K+ transporter is an exception, with a RCK domain dimer as the functional unit (Roosild et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior structural studies.

claim: The KefC K+ transporter is an exception, with a RCK domain dimer as the functional unit.
source: RCK domains form dimeric or pseudo-dimeric units (Jiang et al., 2001; Wu et al., 2010; Yuan et al., 2010), which assemble as functional octameric rings (Albright et al., 2006; Jiang et al., 2002; Wu et al., 2010; Yuan et al., 2010); the KefC K+ transporter is an exception, with a RCK domain dimer as the functional unit (Roosild et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The regulatory role of RCK domains results from the rearrangement of the dimer unit upon binding of signaling molecules.
source: The regulatory role of RCK domains results from the rearrangement of the dimer unit upon binding of signaling molecules, which ultimately causes a conformational change in the effector membrane protein.
evidence: This is a general mechanistic principle supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: RCK domains are classified as either nucleotide- or cation-dependent.
source: In general, RCK domains are classified as either nucleotide- or cation-dependent (Cao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: BK or Slo1 is activated by Ca2+.
source: The eukaryotic Slo K+ channels are regulated by cation-dependent RCK domains: BK or Slo1 is activated by Ca2+, Slo2 by Na+ and Slo3 is pH-dependent.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Slo2 is activated by Na+.
source: The eukaryotic Slo K+ channels are regulated by cation-dependent RCK domains: BK or Slo1 is activated by Ca2+, Slo2 by Na+ and Slo3 is pH-dependent.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Slo3 is pH-dependent.
source: The eukaryotic Slo K+ channels are regulated by cation-dependent RCK domains: BK or Slo1 is activated by Ca2+, Slo2 by Na+ and Slo3 is pH-dependent.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The mechanism of RCK activation in BK by Ca2+ is particularly well understood.
source: The mechanism of RCK activation in BK by Ca2+ is particularly well understood; divalent cations bind to sites formed in the activated state of the ring, stabilizing this conformation and opening the ion channel gate (Hite et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In BK channels, divalent cations bind to sites formed in the activated state of the ring, stabilizing this conformation and opening the ion channel gate.
source: The mechanism of RCK activation in BK by Ca2+ is particularly well understood; divalent cations bind to sites formed in the activated state of the ring, stabilizing this conformation and opening the ion channel gate (Hite et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Ca2+ stabilizes the MthK RCK octameric ring and activates the channel in a cooperative manner.
source: Ca2+ stabilizes the RCK octameric ring and activates the channel in a cooperative manner (Dong et al., 2005; Pau et al., 2010; Ye et al., 2006; Zadek and Nimigean, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: H+ binding disrupts the MthK RCK octameric ring.
source: In contrast, H+ binding disrupts the RCK octameric ring (Dong et al., 2005; Ye et al., 2006) and inhibits activation of the channel (Pau et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: H+ binding inhibits activation of the MthK channel.
source: In contrast, H+ binding disrupts the RCK octameric ring (Dong et al., 2005; Ye et al., 2006) and inhibits activation of the channel (Pau et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Three distinct Ca2+ binding sites have been identified in each MthK RCK domain.
source: Three distinct Ca2+ binding sites have been identified in each MthK RCK domain, six sites per dimeric unit.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge from prior structural studies.

claim: All Ca2+ binding sites in MthK are involved in channel activation.
source: All sites are involved in channel activation, and some are allosterically coupled (Pau et al., 2011; Smith et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Some Ca2+ binding sites in MthK are allosterically coupled.
source: All sites are involved in channel activation, and some are allosterically coupled (Pau et al., 2011; Smith et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In MthK, some of the Ca2+ sites are at protein interfaces so that cation binding alters the conformation of the RCK dimeric unit.
source: Like in the BK channel, some of the Ca2+ sites are at protein interfaces so that cation binding alters the conformation of the RCK dimeric unit, stabilizing the ring in an activated state and opening the channel (Smith et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The molecular mechanisms that underlie ligand-dependent conformational changes in nucleotide-activated RCK domains are not well understood.
source: Unlike cation-dependent RCK domains, the molecular mechanisms that underlie ligand-dependent conformational changes in nucleotide-activated RCK domains are not well understood.
evidence: This represents a knowledge gap that the study aims to address.

claim: KtrAB is a cation channel with a nucleotide-dependent RCK domain.
source: KtrAB is a cation channel with a nucleotide-dependent RCK domain.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the KtrAB system.

claim: KtrAB is an essential component of the K+ homeostasis machinery in many bacteria.
source: This channel is an essential component of the K+ homeostasis machinery in many bacteria, involved in adaptation to osmotic stress and in pH regulation (Holtmann et al., 2003; Ochrombel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The structure of the KtrAB complex revealed a homodimeric membrane protein (KtrB) assembled with a cytosolic RCK octameric ring, formed by the KtrA protein.
source: The structure of the KtrAB complex revealed a homodimeric membrane protein (KtrB) assembled with a cytosolic RCK octameric ring, formed by the KtrA protein (Diskowski et al., 2017; Vieira-Pires et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: KtrA binds nucleotides, ATP or ADP.
source: KtrA binds nucleotides, ATP or ADP.
evidence: This is established knowledge about KtrA.

claim: ATP binding induces the adoption of a square-conformation by the KtrA octameric ring and increased K+ flux activity through KtrAB.
source: ATP binding induces the adoption of a square-conformation by the octameric ring and increased K+ flux activity through KtrAB; ADP binding results in a non-square conformation and decreased flux (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1a and prior research.

claim: ADP binding results in a non-square conformation and decreased flux.
source: ATP binding induces the adoption of a square-conformation by the octameric ring and increased K+ flux activity through KtrAB; ADP binding results in a non-square conformation and decreased flux (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1a and prior research.

claim: It is not clear how ATP binding induces the activated conformation of the RCK ring.
source: However, it is still not clear how ATP binding induces the activated conformation of the RCK ring.
evidence: This represents a knowledge gap that the study aims to address.

claim: The adoption of the square conformation upon ATP binding involves a change in the intra-dimer hinge angle.
source: As previously described (Albright et al., 2006; Rocha et al., 2019; Vieira-Pires et al., 2013), the adoption of the square conformation upon ATP binding involves a change in the intra-dimer hinge angle (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research and structural data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The change in intra-dimer hinge angle brings closer together the two nucleotide-binding sites in the RCK dimeric units.
source: This change brings closer together the two nucleotide-binding sites in the RCK dimeric units, as seen in the D36-D36 Cα intra-dimer distance, a conserved residue in the nucleotide binding site (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Narrowing of the intra-dimer space with bound ATP allows the establishment of interactions between the phosphate groups and residues in both the same and opposite subunits of the KtrA dimer.
source: Narrowing of the intra-dimer space with bound ATP allows the establishment of interactions between the phosphate groups and residues in both the same and opposite subunits of the KtrA dimer (Figure 1a and b).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1a and b.

claim: The R16 residues are positioned between the two nucleotides and appear to stabilize the closely positioned negatively-charged phosphate groups.
source: In particular, the R16 residues are positioned between the two nucleotides and appear to stabilize the closely positioned negatively-charged phosphate groups.
evidence: This is based on structural observations from the ATP-bound structure.

claim: In the ADP-bound structure the nucleotide molecules do not establish interactions with opposing subunit residues.
source: In contrast, in the ADP-bound structure the nucleotide molecules do not establish interactions with opposing subunit residues.
evidence: This is based on structural observations from the ADP-bound structure.

claim: Bridging interactions mediated by R16 and ATP stabilize the square or high-flux conformation of the KtrA octameric ring.
source: Based on this evidence, we previously proposed that bridging interactions mediated by R16 and ATP stabilize the square or high-flux conformation of the KtrA octameric ring (Vieira-Pires et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior work that is being tested in this study.

claim: Expression of wild-type KtrAB allows growth of TK2420 in only 1 mM K+.
source: While empty vector-containing cells require a minimum of 30 mM K+, expression of wild-type KtrAB allows growth of TK2420 in only 1 mM K+ (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Empty vector-containing TK2420 cells require a minimum of 30 mM K+ for growth.
source: While empty vector-containing cells require a minimum of 30 mM K+, expression of wild-type KtrAB allows growth of TK2420 in only 1 mM K+ (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The A80P mutation resulted in KtrAB inactivation.
source: As expected, A80P resulted in KtrAB inactivation.
evidence: This is supported by data from the complementation assay shown in Figure 2.

claim: None of the R16 mutations had an impact on the growth phenotype.
source: However, and contrary to our predictions, none of the R16 mutations had an impact on the growth phenotype, while E125Q resulted in an apparently inactive KtrAB (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by data from the complementation assay shown in Figure 2.

claim: E125Q resulted in an apparently inactive KtrAB.
source: However, and contrary to our predictions, none of the R16 mutations had an impact on the growth phenotype, while E125Q resulted in an apparently inactive KtrAB (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by data from the complementation assay shown in Figure 2.

claim: The KtrA mutants A80P and E125Q assemble as octamers.
source: Both mutants assemble as octamers and are able to form a stable complex with KtrB, as revealed by size-exclusion chromatography (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a and b).
evidence: This is supported by size-exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The KtrA mutants A80P and E125Q are able to form a stable complex with KtrB.
source: Both mutants assemble as octamers and are able to form a stable complex with KtrB, as revealed by size-exclusion chromatography (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a and b).
evidence: This is supported by size-exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The structures of R16K and R16A with ATP are very similar to that of the previously determined wild-type KtrA-ATP.
source: The structures of R16K (at 2.7 Å resolution) and R16A (at 3.4 Å resolution) with ATP are very similar to that of the previously determined wild-type KtrA-ATP (WT-ATP) (Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), adopting the square conformation.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: R16K and R16A with ATP adopt the square conformation.
source: The structures of R16K (at 2.7 Å resolution) and R16A (at 3.4 Å resolution) with ATP are very similar to that of the previously determined wild-type KtrA-ATP (WT-ATP) (Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), adopting the square conformation.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the ATP-bound rings, the L1/L2 distances are similar in the R16K (30.8/30.8 Å), R16A (29.9/29.9 Å) mutants and wild-type (30.0/30.0 Å) structures.
source: In the ATP-bound rings, these distances are similar in the R16K (30.8/30.8 Å), R16A (29.9/29.9 Å) mutants and wild-type (30.0/30.0 Å) structures.
evidence: This is supported by structural measurements from the crystal structures.

claim: The ADP-bound R16K and R16A rings adopt a non-square conformation.
source: Like in the wild-type protein, the ADP-bound R16K (at 3.0 Å resolution) and R16A (at 3.7 Å resolution) rings adopt a non-square conformation (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The ADP-bound ring conformations of R16K and R16A are different from each other and from the wild-type.
source: However, the ADP-bound ring conformations are different from each other and from the wild-type, with L1/L2 distances for the wild-type of 40.7/30.7 Å and for R16K of 52.0/21.9 Å (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by structural measurements from the crystal structures.

claim: KtrA mutants that show a wild-type protein function (R16K and R16A) are able to adopt a square conformation with ATP.
source: KtrA mutants that show a wild-type protein function (R16K and R16A) are able to adopt a square conformation with ATP.
evidence: This is supported by structural data and functional assays.

claim: Mutants that do not rescue growth (A80P and E125Q) do not adopt the square conformation in the ATP-bound structures.
source: In contrast, mutants that do not rescue growth (A80P and E125Q) also do not adopt the square conformation in the ATP-bound structures.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: KtrAB activation requires the adoption of a stable KtrA-ATP ring square conformation.
source: Overall, these results confirm that KtrAB activation requires the adoption of a stable KtrA-ATP ring square conformation.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the correlation between square conformation and functional activity.

claim: A80 and E125 are crucial residues in the adoption of the square conformation.
source: Importantly, they also reveal that, while R16 does not play a major role in the mechanism, A80 and E125 are crucial residues in the adoption of this conformation.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the structural and functional data for the mutants.

claim: The A80P mutation causes a distortion of the main-chain and leads to an alteration in the position of the ATP.
source: We concluded therefore that the A80P mutation causes a distortion of the main-chain and leads to an alteration in the position of the ATP, impeding the adoption of the square conformation.
evidence: This is based on analysis of electron density maps shown in Figure 4.

claim: In the 2.7 Å structure of the ATP-bound R16K KtrA mutant, there was a distinct additional electron-density in the KtrA intra-dimer interface, between the γ-phosphates of the nucleotide.
source: A clue for the role of E125 is revealed by the 2.7 Å structure of the ATP-bound R16K KtrA mutant. In this structure, there was a distinct additional electron-density in the KtrA intra-dimer interface, between the γ-phosphates of the nucleotide (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The density in the R16K structure likely corresponds to a magnesium ion.
source: After careful crystallographic refinement, we concluded that the density likely corresponds to a magnesium ion (Figure 5a and b).
evidence: This is based on crystallographic analysis and coordination geometry.

claim: The magnesium ion is coordinated by six oxygen atoms, adopting octahedral geometry.
source: The ion is coordinated by six oxygen atoms, adopting octahedral geometry.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The coordinating atoms for the magnesium ion are provided by the γ-phosphate of both ATP molecules, by two water molecules and by the carboxylic groups of the two E125 residues.
source: The coordinating atoms are provided by the γ-phosphate of both ATP molecules, by two water molecules and by the carboxylic groups of the two E125 residues.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Mg2+ was not added to the protein or crystallization mixture and so the ion was sequestered during protein preparation or crystallization.
source: It is worthwhile mentioning that Mg2+ was not added to the protein or crystallization mixture and so the ion was sequestered during protein preparation or crystallization.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental conditions.

claim: It is possible to detect density in the wild-type KtrA structure bound to ATP (PDB code: 4J90) that could be accounted by a coordinated Mg2+.
source: We revisited the electron-density maps of the previously resolved wild-type KtrA structure bound to ATP (at 3.2 Å, PDB code: 4J90), which also adopts a square-conformation, looking for unexplained density in the intra-dimer interface. It is possible to detect density that could also be accounted by a coordinated Mg2+ (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by re-analysis of electron density maps shown in Figure 5c.

claim: In the wild-type structure, the magnesium cation has a similar octahedral coordination to that seen in the R16K mutant structure.
source: Re-refinement of the structure with Mg2+ does not cause great adjustments in the intra-dimer interface. The cation has a similar octahedral coordination to that seen in the R16K mutant structure, interacting with the oxygen atoms in the γ-phosphate of both ATP molecules and the carboxylic groups of the E125 residues.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: In the wild-type structure, nitrogen atoms of the R16 guanidinium group appear to complete the coordination shell of the divalent cation.
source: However, instead of water molecules, nitrogen atoms of the R16 guanidinium group appear to complete the coordination shell of the divalent cation (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: E125 coordinates Mg2+ at the intra-dimer interface.
source: Overall, these structural results reveal that E125 coordinates Mg2+ at the intra-dimer interface.
evidence: This is supported by structural data from multiple structures.

claim: The γ-phosphates of the ATP molecules complete the coordination of the divalent cation.
source: Importantly, the γ-phosphates of the ATP molecules complete the coordination of the divalent cation.
evidence: This is supported by structural data from multiple structures.

claim: The divalent cation bridges the ligand molecules in two KtrA subunits.
source: In this arrangement, the divalent cation bridges the ligand molecules in two KtrA subunits, suggesting that the cation stabilizes the two subunits in the RCK dimers close together, favoring the adoption of the square conformation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural arrangement observed.

claim: The divalent cation stabilizes the two subunits in the RCK dimers close together, favoring the adoption of the square conformation.
source: In this arrangement, the divalent cation bridges the ligand molecules in two KtrA subunits, suggesting that the cation stabilizes the two subunits in the RCK dimers close together, favoring the adoption of the square conformation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural arrangement observed.

claim: Mutation of E125 to glutamine likely affects the coordination of the Mg2+ binding site, changing the stability of the square conformation.
source: Mutation to glutamine likely affects the coordination of the Mg2+ binding site, changing the stability of the square conformation and explaining the inability of the E125Q KtrA mutant to rescue the TK2420 phenotype.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural role of E125 and the functional data.

claim: Flux is ~10 fold faster in the presence of Mg2+ for KtrAB-ATP.
source: Flux is ~10 fold faster in the presence of Mg2+, with the rate constant increasing from 0.011 ± 0.001 to 0.096 ± 0.008 s−1 (Figure 6c and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by flux assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Relative to KtrAB-ATP with Mg2+, flux was 14-fold slower for KtrAB-ADP with Mg2+.
source: Relative to KtrAB-ATP with Mg2+, flux was 14-fold and 24-fold slower for KtrAB-ADP and KtrAE125QB-ATP with Mg2+, respectively (Figure 6c and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by flux assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Relative to KtrAB-ATP with Mg2+, flux was 24-fold slower for KtrAE125QB-ATP with Mg2+.
source: Relative to KtrAB-ATP with Mg2+, flux was 14-fold and 24-fold slower for KtrAB-ADP and KtrAE125QB-ATP with Mg2+, respectively (Figure 6c and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by flux assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Mg2+ also activates the complex with the R16A KtrA mutant.
source: Like for wild-type KtrAB-ATP, Mg2+ also activates the complex with the R16A KtrA mutant (Figure 6b and c, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by flux assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Absence of added divalent cation did not abolish KtrAB-ATP activity.
source: Despite the clear impact of Mg2+, it is noticeable that absence of added divalent cation did not abolish KtrAB-ATP activity and that its flux is larger than for KtrB or KtrAB-ADP (Figure 6a and c).
evidence: This is supported by flux assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Adding 0.7 or 2 mM Ca2+ or Mg2+ increases flux up to 4-fold relative to the condition without divalent cation.
source: Relative to the condition without divalent cation, adding 0.7 or 2 mM Ca2+ or Mg2+ increases flux up to 4-fold.
evidence: This is supported by flux assay data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Rate constants with 2 mM Mg2+ or 2 mM Ca2+ become similar to those measured in the sorbitol/Mg2+ condition.
source: Rate constants become similar to those measured in the sorbitol/Mg2+ condition (0.088 ± 0.0.002 s−1 for 2 mM Mg2+ and 0.092 ± 0.001 s−1 for 2 mM Ca2+) (Figure 7a and b and Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by flux assay data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The flux rate constant with 5 mM Mg2+ is unchanged, but it decreases 9-fold with 5 mM Ca2+.
source: However, while the flux rate constant with 5 mM Mg2+ is unchanged, it decreases 9-fold with 5 mM Ca2+ (Figure 7b and Figure 7—source data 1), suggesting that, at high concentrations, Ca2+ inhibits flux by blocking the KtrAB channel.
evidence: This is supported by flux assay data shown in Figure 7.

claim: At high concentrations, Ca2+ inhibits flux by blocking the KtrAB channel.
source: However, while the flux rate constant with 5 mM Mg2+ is unchanged, it decreases 9-fold with 5 mM Ca2+ (Figure 7b and Figure 7—source data 1), suggesting that, at high concentrations, Ca2+ inhibits flux by blocking the KtrAB channel.
evidence: This is an inference based on the flux assay data.

claim: The structure of wild-type KtrA-ATP crystallized in the presence of 5 mM Ca2+ shows an octameric ring adopting a square conformation.
source: In addition, we crystallized wild-type KtrA-ATP in the presence of 5 mM of Ca2+ and determined the structure at 3.0 Å resolution (Figure 7c and Table 1). The structure shows an octameric ring adopting a square conformation with L1/L2 distances of 30.5/30.5 Å that are similar to those of the WT-ATP structure (Supplementary file 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 7c and Table 1.

claim: The intra-dimer interface of the Ca2+-bound structure shows a bound calcium ion.
source: The intra-dimer interface shows a bound calcium ion (Figure 7d).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 7d.

claim: The calcium ion coordination shell is formed by oxygens from the carboxylic groups of the E125 side chains and the oxygen atoms of the ATP γ-phosphates.
source: After refinement, we defined a coordination shell formed by oxygens from the carboxylic groups of the E125 side chains and the oxygen atoms of the ATP γ-phosphates.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 7d.

claim: The intra-dimer interface site binds both Mg2+ and Ca2+.
source: These functional and structural experiments establish that the intra-dimer interface site binds both Mg2+and Ca2+, further supporting the idea that divalent cations stabilize the square conformation of the RCK domain ring and activate the KtrAB.
evidence: This is supported by structural and functional data.

claim: Fluorescence quenching in the presence of 150 mM choline chloride was comparable to the sorbitol/Mg2+ condition.
source: We were surprised to observe that fluorescence quenching was comparable to the sorbitol/Mg2+ condition above, with steady-state values of ~80% and a rate constant of 0.062 ± 0.007 s−1 (Figure 8a and c and Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by flux assay data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Addition of Mg2+ to 150 mM choline chloride had little or no effect on the rate constant.
source: Addition of Mg2+ had little or no effect in the rate constant (0.058 ± 0.003 or 0.079 ± 0.010 s−1 with addition of 0.7 mM or 2 mM Mg2+, respectively), confirming that KtrAB is fully active in the presence of 150 mM choline chloride (Figure 8a and c and Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by flux assay data shown in Figure 8.

claim: KtrAB is active in the absence of Cl- as the rate constants in choline acetate and choline chloride are similar.
source: To explore the role of Cl- we performed the functional assay with 150 mM choline acetate (Figure 8—figure supplement 1) and concluded that KtrAB is active in the absence of Cl- as the rate constants in choline acetate (0.043 ± 0.002 s−1) and choline chloride are similar.
evidence: This is supported by flux assay data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: KtrAE125QB-ATP and KtrAB-ADP display low ion flux in the presence of 150 mM choline.
source: Both KtrAE125QB-ATP and KtrAB-ADP display low ion flux, with rates that are 12- and 16-fold slower than for KtrAB-ATP (Figure 8b and c and Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by flux assay data shown in Figure 8.

claim: KtrAR16AB-ATP is active in the choline condition without added Mg2+.
source: In contrast, KtrAR16AB-ATP is also active in the choline condition without added Mg2+ (Figure 8b and c).
evidence: This is supported by flux assay data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The contaminating levels of Mg2+ in the choline solution are undetectable (less than 2 µM).
source: Importantly, using flame ionization spectroscopy we determined that the contaminating levels of Mg2+ in the choline solution are undetectable (less than 2 µM), which as shown further down is well below the activating concentrations for this divalent cation.
evidence: This is supported by flame ionization spectroscopy measurements.

claim: Choline is able to activate KtrAB and the effect is exerted through the RCK domain ring, involving the same intra-dimer interface site identified for Mg2+.
source: Overall, these data suggest that choline is able to activate KtrAB and that the effect is exerted through the RCK domain ring, involving the same intra-dimer interface site identified for Mg2+.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional data with choline and mutants.

claim: In the presence of 5 and 20 mM Li+, flux is higher than in sorbitol alone (~2 and ~5 fold, respectively).
source: In the presence of 5 and 20 mM Li+, flux is higher than in sorbitol alone (~2 and~5 fold, respectively) (Figure 9 and Figure 9—source data 1, confront (cf.) with Figure 6c).
evidence: This is supported by flux assay data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Addition of Mg2+ to 5 or 20 mM Li+ results in a 3- and 1.5-fold increase in the rate constants.
source: Addition of Mg2+ to either one of these conditions results in a 3- and 1.5-fold increase in the rate constants (0.069 ± 0.001 and 0.070 ± 0.002 s−1, respectively), similar to the maximum observed above (cf. Figure 6c).
evidence: This is supported by flux assay data shown in Figure 9.

claim: KtrAE125QB-ATP or KtrB-ATP in the presence of 20 mM Li+ display rates that are ~12 and ~15 fold lower than KtrAB-ATP in the same condition.
source: Importantly, KtrAE125QB-ATP or KtrB-ATP in the presence of 20 mM Li+ display rates that are ~12 and~15 fold lower than KtrAB-ATP in the same condition, suggesting that the Li+ effect is mediated by the RCK domain (Figure 9).
evidence: This is supported by flux assay data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The Li+ effect is mediated by the RCK domain.
source: Importantly, KtrAE125QB-ATP or KtrB-ATP in the presence of 20 mM Li+ display rates that are ~12 and~15 fold lower than KtrAB-ATP in the same condition, suggesting that the Li+ effect is mediated by the RCK domain (Figure 9).
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional data with Li+ and mutants.

claim: Monovalent cations (both Li+ and choline) are able to activate KtrAB through a mechanism that involves the intra-dimer interface of the RCK domain.
source: Overall, our data suggest that monovalent cations (both Li+ and choline) are able to activate KtrAB through a mechanism that involves the intra-dimer interface of the RCK domain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional data with monovalent cations and mutants.

claim: The K1/2 of activation for Mg2+ is 155 ± 17 µM with a Hill coefficient of 1.8 ± 0.0.
source: Fitting the titration curves with a Hill equation yielded a K1/2 of activation for Mg2+ of 155 ± 17 µM (Hill coefficient 1.8 ± 0.0) and for choline, 25 ± 2 mM for choline with a Hill coefficient 1.9 ± 0.2 (Figure 10b and d).
evidence: This is supported by titration data shown in Figure 10.

claim: The K1/2 of activation for choline is 25 ± 2 mM with a Hill coefficient of 1.9 ± 0.2.
source: Fitting the titration curves with a Hill equation yielded a K1/2 of activation for Mg2+ of 155 ± 17 µM (Hill coefficient 1.8 ± 0.0) and for choline, 25 ± 2 mM for choline with a Hill coefficient 1.9 ± 0.2 (Figure 10b and d).
evidence: This is supported by titration data shown in Figure 10.

claim: The KtrAB activation mechanism is ~160 fold more sensitive to Mg2+ than choline.
source: Nevertheless, we clearly show that the KtrAB activation mechanism is ~160 fold more sensitive to Mg2+ than choline.
evidence: This is based on the comparison of K1/2 values for Mg2+ and choline.

claim: The structure of KtrA from M. jannaschii clearly shows a glutamate residue in the same position as E125 in KtrA from B. subtilis.
source: First, we analyzed the structure of the KtrA protein from the thermophilic archaean Methanocaldococcus jannaschii (PDB:1LSS) (Figure 11a). The structure clearly shows a glutamate residue in the same position as E125 in KtrA from B. subtilis.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 11a.

claim: 13 out of 15 KtrA orthologs have a glutamate coincident with E125, corresponding to 87% sequence identity.
source: The final alignment has 15 sequences, including KtrA from B. subtilis, of which 13 have a glutamate coincident with E125, corresponding to 87% sequence identity.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 11b.

claim: A neighboring proline to E125 is also highly conserved, forming the motif PE.
source: Interestingly, a neighboring proline is also highly conserved, forming the motif PE.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 11b.

claim: In TrkA, there is a glutamate in RCK1 in a position similar to that of E125 in KtrA.
source: We also inspected the TrkA protein from Vibrio parahaemolyticus (PDB:4J9V); this protein assembles with the membrane protein TrkH to form the non-selective TrkHA cation channel (Figure 11c). TrkA has two RCK domains in tandem (RCK1 and RCK2), forming a pseudo-dimeric unit, and both domains bind nucleotide. In the intra-dimer interface there is a glutamate in RCK1 in a position similar to that of E125 in KtrA.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 11c.

claim: In TrkA RCK2, there is a glutamine in the position equivalent to E125.
source: In contrast, in RCK2 there is a glutamine.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 11c.

claim: The PE sequence motif is highly conserved in TrkA RCK1 (80% sequence identity).
source: A sequence alignment of TrkA orthologs generated using the approach described above shows that the PE sequence motif noted in KtrA is highly conserved in RCK1 (80% sequence identity) (Figure 11d and Figure 11—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 11d.

claim: There are no glutamates or aspartates in the E125 position of TrkA RCK2 in any of the orthologs.
source: However, there are no glutamates or aspartates in the E125 position of RCK2 in any of the orthologs (Figure 11—figure supplement 3); instead, arginine and lysine residues are common, strongly suggesting that in TrkA the activation mechanism is not dependent on a divalent cation cofactor.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 3.

claim: In TrkA the activation mechanism is not dependent on a divalent cation cofactor.
source: However, there are no glutamates or aspartates in the E125 position of RCK2 in any of the orthologs (Figure 11—figure supplement 3); instead, arginine and lysine residues are common, strongly suggesting that in TrkA the activation mechanism is not dependent on a divalent cation cofactor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sequence analysis.

claim: The structure of the C-terminal domain of KefC from E. coli shows a glutamate at the intra-dimer interface, shifted one residue in the sequence relative to KtrA.
source: Despite these differences, the structure of the C-terminal domain of KefC from E. coli shows the homo-dimeric unit arrangement and an AMP molecule bound in a similar binding site to KtrA (Figure 11e). Strikingly, the KefC structure shows a glutamate at the intra-dimer interface, shifted one residue in the sequence relative to KtrA.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 11e.

claim: A sequence alignment of 11 KefC proteins shows that the glutamate at the intra-dimer interface is 100% conserved.
source: A sequence alignment of the C termini of 11 KefC proteins shows that the glutamate at the intra-dimer interface is 100% conserved (Figure 11f and Figure 11—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 11f.

claim: The sequence motif in KefC is RE or TE, and not PE as seen in KtrA.
source: The sequence motif is RE or TE, and not PE as seen in KtrA.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 11f.

claim: The structure of YbaL shows the presence of a glutamate in the intra-dimer interface in an equivalent position to that of E125 in KtrA.
source: Finally, we analyzed the structure of the nucleotide-dependent RCK domain of YbaL (PDB: 3FWZ), a putative E. coli cation antiporter. As stated above, YbaL proteins are related to KefC. This structure also shows the presence of a glutamate in the intra-dimer interface in an equivalent position to that of E125 in KtrA (Figure 11g).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 11g.

claim: A sequence alignment of YbaL orthologs reveals that the glutamate is strongly conserved (100% conserved among the 12 sequences).
source: A sequence alignment reveals that the glutamate is strongly conserved (100% conserved among the 12 sequences) but the sequence motif is primarily GE instead of PE (Figure 11h and Figure 11—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 11h.

claim: The sequence motif in YbaL is primarily GE instead of PE.
source: A sequence alignment reveals that the glutamate is strongly conserved (100% conserved among the 12 sequences) but the sequence motif is primarily GE instead of PE (Figure 11h and Figure 11—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 11h.

claim: There is a striking conservation of glutamates in the intra-dimer interface of many homodimeric nucleotide-dependent RCK domains.
source: This analysis reveals a striking conservation of glutamates in the intra-dimer interface of many homodimeric nucleotide-dependent RCK domains.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the sequence and structural analysis across multiple RCK domain families.

claim: The conserved glutamates occupy similar positions to E125 in KtrA.
source: These glutamates occupy similar positions to E125 in KtrA, strongly suggesting that the cation-binding site is present in many nucleotide-dependent RCK domains and in particular, that divalent cations are essential cofactors for the activation of these RCK proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conservation analysis.

claim: The cation-binding site is present in many nucleotide-dependent RCK domains.
source: These glutamates occupy similar positions to E125 in KtrA, strongly suggesting that the cation-binding site is present in many nucleotide-dependent RCK domains and in particular, that divalent cations are essential cofactors for the activation of these RCK proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conservation analysis.

claim: In the cell, the active conformation of the RCK domain ring in KtrAB will involve Mg2+ and not Ca2+.
source: It is therefore reasonable to think that in the cell, the active conformation of the RCK domain ring in KtrAB will involve Mg2+ and not Ca2+.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relative concentrations of Mg2+ and Ca2+ in bacterial cells.

claim: The free concentration of K+ in the cytosol is sufficient to make a contribution to the activation of KtrAB.
source: However, the reported K+ concentration in the cytosol of B. subtilis is ~300 mM, rising to 600–700 mM in certain environmental conditions (Whatmore et al., 1990). It is therefore likely that the free concentration of the monovalent cation in the cytosol is sufficient to make a contribution to the activation of KtrAB.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reported K+ concentrations and the activation data.

claim: There is a single well defined square or active conformation for KtrA.
source: This indicates that there is a single well defined square or active conformation for KtrA, while the ring in the non-active (or non-square) conformation is most likely more flexible, giving rise to different ring conformations in the crystals of isolated KtrA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural comparison of multiple KtrA structures.

claim: The ring in the non-active (or non-square) conformation is most likely more flexible.
source: This indicates that there is a single well defined square or active conformation for KtrA, while the ring in the non-active (or non-square) conformation is most likely more flexible, giving rise to different ring conformations in the crystals of isolated KtrA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural variability observed in non-square conformations.
